title: New Trial Finds Stopping Statins After 75 May Be Safe for Low-Risk Adults
excerpt: The first randomized controlled trial on statin discontinuation in healthy older adults showed similar three-year survival rates — but experts say the study may be too small to settle the debate.
body:
• A new randomized controlled trial found that adults over 75 who stopped taking statins had similar three-year survival rates to those who continued the medication, marking the first RCT evidence on this question.
  • The trial enrolled approximately 1,200 participants at low cardiovascular risk who had been on statins for primary prevention, with 36 months of follow-up.
  • Experts caution the trial may be underpowered to detect differences in cardiovascular events, and larger ongoing trials like STAREE and PREVENTABLE are expected to provide more definitive answers.
  • For South Asian older adults — a population with elevated baseline cardiovascular risk — the findings underscore the importance of individualized conversations with doctors rather than blanket discontinuation.

A landmark randomized controlled trial has found that stopping statin therapy in adults over 75 who are at low risk for heart disease did not lead to increased deaths over three years, challenging long-held assumptions about the necessity of continuing cholesterol-lowering drugs indefinitely in older populations.

The study, one of the first RCTs to directly test statin discontinuation in otherwise healthy elderly patients, enrolled roughly 1,200 participants who had been taking statins for primary prevention — meaning they had no prior history of heart attack or stroke. Half continued their medication; the other half stopped. Over three years, survival rates between the two groups were statistically similar.

Why This Trial Matters

Until now, evidence on statins in older adults has been dominated by observational studies, which carry inherent limitations. A widely cited 2019 French cohort study of 120,173 patients found that discontinuing statins at age 75 was associated with a 33% increased risk of cardiovascular hospitalization. But observational data cannot fully account for the reasons people stop taking medication — sicker patients, for instance, may be more likely to discontinue.

This new RCT provides the first randomized evidence that for low-risk older adults specifically, stopping statins may not carry the penalty those observational studies suggested. The distinction is critical: the trial focused on patients without established cardiovascular disease and with relatively few risk factors.

The Caveats

Several experts have flagged the trial as potentially underpowered — meaning it may have been too small to detect meaningful differences in heart attacks or strokes, even if they exist. With roughly 1,200 participants and a three-year follow-up, the study was designed primarily around mortality, not individual cardiovascular events.

"The results are reassuring but should not be taken as a green light for wholesale statin discontinuation in older adults."

— Cardiovascular medicine experts

Larger trials currently underway are expected to provide more definitive guidance. STAREE, a randomized placebo-controlled trial based in Australia, is evaluating atorvastatin in adults 70 and older without cardiovascular disease, with results anticipated in the coming years. PREVENTABLE, another major RCT, is examining statin benefits beyond cardiovascular outcomes, including effects on cognitive decline and dementia.

What This Means for South Asian Older Adults

The findings carry particular nuance for the South Asian diaspora. Research has consistently shown that South Asians face elevated cardiovascular risk compared to other ethnic groups, with higher rates of coronary artery disease, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome — often manifesting at younger ages. The trial's focus on "low-risk" patients may therefore apply to a smaller subset of South Asian older adults than the general population.

For aging parents and grandparents in the diaspora community, the takeaway is not to stop statins unilaterally. Rather, the trial reinforces the value of having an individualized risk conversation with a physician, particularly for those who have been on statins for years without a cardiovascular event.

The Bigger Picture

The debate over statins in older adults sits at the intersection of two realities. On one hand, polypharmacy — the use of multiple medications — is a growing concern for elderly patients, with each additional drug carrying potential side effects and interactions. On the other, cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death globally, and statins are among the most well-studied preventive medications in medical history.

Current guidelines from the American College of Cardiology acknowledge the uncertainty, suggesting that statin discontinuation "may be reasonable" for older patients with limited life expectancy, significant frailty, or multiple comorbidities. This new trial adds a data point — but not yet a conclusive one — to a conversation that millions of families are having at kitchen tables and doctor's offices worldwide.
